description: Solo participant from Trujillo, Peru, looking for 2–3 teammates. I’m an industrial engineering student with a background in physics (optics and spectroscopy lab work), operations research, Monte Carlo simulation and Python/MATLAB. We will build an interactive mission design game with real orbital dynamics (three-body problem and trajectory sensitivity). We are looking for: a web/front-end developer, a game or UX designer, and someone with video and storytelling skills.
summary:
I grew up in Peru reading about Pedro Paulet, the Arequipa engineer who claimed to fire a liquid-fuel rocket engine in the 1890s, and like many kids I dreamed of NASA: of being an astronaut, or the engineer behind the launch. Paulet — Andes to Orbit is the game I wish I had then. You are Dr. Pedro Goicochea, a fictional Peruvian physicist who swears to finish what Paulet began, and his letters to Paulet tell the story in first person. The fiction stands on real history (Paulet’s Avión-Torpedo, Goddard, Apollo, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Perseverance, all cited in the game) and feels like home: a launch base under the Misti volcano, Kuntur, a condor robot named in Quechua, and quena and charango over space synths.

Under the story is a real mission design game for one to four players, online or on one screen. The team designs a whole mission (objective, spacecraft, instruments, orbit, launcher), negotiates a shared budget, votes, launches in a 3D flight deck and flies a seeded simulation where each player decides their own role’s events. Every choice moves at least two resources (mass, power, data, budget, schedule, lifetime), and the report explains why the mission worked or failed.

Everything was made for this game: story, characters, code and even the songs, with lyrics we wrote (the AI tools we used are disclosed below). It runs in the browser, offline after the first visit, in English and Spanish, with no account.
details:
1. Define the mission. Each scenario starts with a client and a goal (for example Earth Watch: monitor forests and crops from orbit), minimum requirements, a budget and a deadline. A short briefing explains what to deliver and why.
  2. Design the spacecraft. Tabs for payload, spacecraft, orbit & launch, and ground & comms. Instruments have mass, power, cost, data rate and science value; subsystems come in simple and advanced versions. A live dashboard shows every resource with +/− changes as you click.
  3. Review. An automatic design review marks each issue green, amber or red and explains the cause and what to change (for example: the spacecraft is heavier than the launcher can lift to that orbit; the downlink cannot carry the data). Red items block the launch.
  4. Play as a team of four. Mission Director (Dr. Goicochea), Spacecraft Engineer (Chicho), Astrophysicist (Roberto) and Astrobiologist (Franchesca). The budget is split by area according to what matters most in each mission, each role has its own goal plus a group goal, and big decisions and the final review go to a vote with veto. Play on one device or online in a shared room joined by link; Kuntur, an Andean condor robot guide, takes any empty seat and answers questions.
  5. Launch. A mission-control flight deck with telemetry for the chosen orbit and live cameras (ground, chase, onboard and a map of the ascent over NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble imagery).
  6. Fly and evaluate. A week-by-week seeded simulation with random events (solar storms, failures, slips) that the team answers together. Score 0–1000 with the three main reasons for the result.
  7. Letter to Paulet. The report arrives as a console transmission: two personal lines from Goicochea, then the technical "why", signed with the value that guided the team (rigor, boldness or service). A failed mission still gets its letter and a retry with the same seed.
  8. Compare and share. A side-by-side trade study of two designs (as in NASA's Mission Design Lab), a per-mission ranking, and challenge links that send friends the same mission and the same random events.

How it works

  • A TypeScript engine (no user-interface code) computes every budget: orbit period and eclipse, launcher capacity per orbit, mass with margins, power from solar arrays and batteries, data volume against downlink, cost and schedule. A seeded random generator makes every mission reproducible, which enables replays, challenge links and fair team comparisons. 250+ automated tests check the formulas.
  • The physics is real and simplified on purpose: the rocket equation per stage, Hohmann transfers and launch windows to Mars, and the Earth–Moon three-body problem for the chaos lesson. Every formula and constant is documented with its NASA source.
  • Scenarios progress from a sounding rocket to Earth orbit, the Moon and Mars, with three difficulty levels (Cadet, Researcher, Program Director).

Benefits

  • Students see the whole system at once instead of one topic at a time, and learn why a design works, not only whether it is correct.
  • Collaboration is built into the rules: roles must negotiate budget and priorities, as real mission teams do.
  • Free, installable, offline after the first visit, bilingual (English/Spanish) and light enough for school laptops, so it can reach classrooms with poor connectivity.

What we hope to achieve

A classroom-ready mission design game that a teacher can open in one minute, and that shows students in Latin America and beyond that space engineering is a path open to them, starting from a story that begins in Arequipa, Peru.

Tools, languages and software

TypeScript, Claude, Google Ai Studio, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand (state), Three.js and postprocessing (3D flight deck), GSAP and Motion (animation), Firebase Realtime Database (online rooms), vite-plugin-pwa (offline play), Vitest (tests), GitHub Actions (continuous integration) and Vercel (hosting). Fonts under the SIL Open Font License.
